key_terms.meaning: D = Et³/[12(1 − ν²)], in N·m; M<sub>x</sub> = D(κ<sub>x</sub> + νκ<sub>y</sub>), M<sub>xy</sub> = D(1 − ν)κ<sub>xy</sub>.
Principal curvatures of opposite sign (saddle) or the same sign (dome); M<sub>x</sub> alone gives κ<sub>y</sub> = −νκ<sub>x</sub>.
D∇⁴w = q + N<sub>x</sub> ∂²w/∂x² + 2N<sub>xy</sub> ∂²w/∂x∂y + N<sub>y</sub> ∂²w/∂y², in-plane forces positive in tension.
Each Navier term grows by 1/(1 − N/N<sub>mn</sub>) under compression N; about 1/(1 − N/N<sub>cr</sub>) overall.
σ<sub>cr</sub> = kπ²E(t/b)²/[12(1 − ν²)], b across the load; k = (m/r + r/m)², minimum 4, for simple supports.
b<sub>e</sub> = 1.90 t √(E/σ<sub>s</sub>), total per stringer; A<sub>e</sub> = A<sub>st</sub> + b<sub>e</sub> t.
σ<sub>cs</sub>/√(σ<sub>cy</sub> E) = C<sub>e</sub>/(b′/t)<sup>0.75</sup>, b′ = (a + b)/2; C<sub>e</sub> = 0.316, 0.342, 0.366 for two, one, no free edges.
σ<sub>cs</sub>/σ<sub>cy</sub> = 0.56[(g t²/A)√(E/σ<sub>cy</sub>)]<sup>0.85</sup> for angles and multi-corner sections; g = flanges + cuts.
P<sub>t</sub> = (GJ + π²EC<sub>w</sub>/L²)/r₀², r₀² = (I<sub>x</sub> + I<sub>y</sub>)/A + x₀² + y₀².
σ<sub>c</sub> = σ<sub>cs</sub>[1 − σ<sub>cs</sub>(L′/ρ)²/(4π²E)], up to L′/ρ = √(2π²E/σ<sub>cs</sub>).

Q<sub>11</sub> = E<sub>1</sub>/(1 − ν<sub>12</sub>ν<sub>21</sub>), Q<sub>12</sub> = ν<sub>12</sub>E<sub>2</sub>/(1 − ν<sub>12</sub>ν<sub>21</sub>), Q<sub>66</sub> = G<sub>12</sub>; ν<sub>21</sub> = ν<sub>12</sub>E<sub>2</sub>/E<sub>1</sub>.
A<sub>ij</sub> = ΣQ̄(z<sub>k</sub> − z<sub>k</sub>−1), B<sub>ij</sub> = ½ΣQ̄(z<sub>k</sub>² − z<sub>k</sub>−1²), D<sub>ij</sub> = ⅓ΣQ̄(z<sub>k</sub>³ − z<sub>k</sub>−1³).
ω<sub>n</sub> = √(k/m), ζ = c/2√(km); resonant amplitude F₀/(2ζk).
q<sub>D</sub> = K_θ/(e S a₁), V<sub>D</sub> = √(2q<sub>D</sub>/ρ), e the aerodynamic centre ahead of the flexural axis.
R<sub>c</sub> + R<sub>s</sub>² = 1 for long flat panels; τ<sub>cr</sub> = k<sub>s</sub>π²E(t/b)²/[12(1 − ν²)], k<sub>s</sub> ≈ 5.35 + 4(b/a)².

takeaways: A thin plate bends through D = Et³/[12(1 − ν²)], and the shape of the bent surface is set by its principal curvatures.
Pressure and in-plane forces enter one plate equation; compression magnifies bending by about 1/(1 − N/N<sub>cr</sub>).
A plate buckles at a stress proportional to (t/b)², with k = 4 for a long simply supported plate and 0.425 for a flange with a free edge.
A buckled skin still carries load in strips next to the stringers, b<sub>e</sub> = 1.90 t √(E/σ<sub>s</sub>) in all per stringer.
Thin-walled sections cripple above their local buckling stress and below yield; Needham and Gerard estimate the crippling stress from b/t.
Open columns with an offset shear centre buckle by bending and twisting together, below their Euler and torsional loads.
A ply is orthotropic and is rotated to structure axes as Q̄; a laminate sums its plies into A, B and D, and B = 0 only if it is symmetric.
Structures resonate at their natural frequencies; aeroelastic coupling gives divergence (static) and flutter (dynamic) speeds.
Compression and shear together follow R<sub>c</sub> + R<sub>s</sub>² = 1 for a long panel; the circle overestimates the allowable shear.
bank_note: Long questions ask for a derivation with its assumptions, or a sizing calculation: a plate buckling stress, an effective width and panel load, a crippling or flexural–torsional buckling load, a laminate stiffness, a natural frequency or divergence speed, or a combined-load margin. State the edge conditions and the sign convention, keep units consistent, and end with a check.

glossary.def: a/b, the panel length along the load over its width across it.
The load at which a second, bent equilibrium appears beside the flat one; the onset of buckling.
An edge held against deflection and rotation: w = 0 and ∂w/∂n = 0.
Local collapse of a thin-walled section after its flat elements have buckled and its corners have yielded.
The rate of change of slope, κ = −∂²w/∂x², in m⁻¹.
Static aeroelastic instability in which the twist of a wing grows without limit at a critical dynamic pressure.
The width of buckled skin which, at the stringer stress, carries the load of the real skin.
Another name for the plate stiffness D.
Dynamic aeroelastic instability: a self-excited oscillation that grows when the net damping becomes negative.
Buckling of skin away from a stringer between two rivets.
One ply of a composite, with all its fibres in one direction.
A stack of bonded plies at chosen angles.
An in-plane force per unit length of a plate, N<sub>x</sub>, N<sub>y</sub> or N<sub>xy</sub>, in N/m.
The surface halfway through the thickness of a plate, from which z is measured.
Having three perpendicular planes of material symmetry, with different stiffness along each axis.
k<sub>r</sub> = ωb/V, the frequency of motion compared with the time the flow takes to cross the semi-chord.
The point through which a transverse load bends a section without twisting it.
The non-uniform direct stress in a wide flange or skin that receives its load by shear from webs.
An edge with no deflection and no bending moment.
A longitudinal stiffener attached to the skin.
A laminate whose plies mirror each other about the mid-plane, so that B = 0.
Out-of-plane displacement of the points of a cross-section under torsion.
Short-wave buckling of skin and attached stringer flange together at the attachment line.

bank.q: Derive the moment–curvature relations and the plate stiffness D for a thin isotropic plate, and explain anticlastic and synclastic bending with sketches. Use a 3 mm aluminium alloy plate to illustrate.
answer: Assumptions (Kirchhoff): the plate is thin, t below about a tenth of its span; normals to the mid-surface stay straight and normal; the mid-surface does not stretch; w is small compared with t; σ<sub>z</sub> is negligible.

answer.text: Strains. A point at height z moves in the plane by u = −z ∂w/∂x, v = −z ∂w/∂y, so:
Stresses in plane stress and moments per unit width, integrating through −t/2 ≤ z ≤ t/2 with ∫z² dz = t³/12:
answer.pre:
σ<sub>x</sub> = E(ε<sub>x</sub> + νε<sub>y</sub>)/(1 − ν²),  τ<sub>xy</sub> = Gγ<sub>xy</sub>
M<sub>x</sub> = ∫σ<sub>x</sub> z dz = D(κ<sub>x</sub> + νκ<sub>y</sub>)
M<sub>y</sub> = D(κ<sub>y</sub> + νκ<sub>x</sub>)
M<sub>xy</sub> = ∫τ<sub>xy</sub> z dz = 2G(t³/12)κ<sub>xy</sub> = D(1 − ν)κ<sub>xy</sub>
D = Et³/[12(1 − ν²)]   (N·m)

answer: Units: E in Pa, t in m, D in N·m; moments in N·m/m. The face stress is σ = 6M/t².

Meaning of 1/(1 − ν²): a plate held flat across (cylindrical bending, κ<sub>y</sub> = 0) develops σ<sub>y</sub> = νσ<sub>x</sub>, and each layer acts with modulus E/(1 − ν²); if free across, κ<sub>y</sub> = −νκ<sub>x</sub> and M<sub>x</sub> = Et³κ<sub>x</sub>/12, the beam value.

Anticlastic bending (sketch a saddle): M<sub>x</sub> alone, M<sub>y</sub> = 0, gives κ<sub>y</sub> = −νκ<sub>x</sub>, so the plate sags along x and hogs across. Pure twist M<sub>xy</sub> gives principal moments ±M<sub>xy</sub> at 45°, also a saddle.

Synclastic bending (sketch a dome): both principal curvatures of one sign, as at the centre of a plate under uniform pressure, or under M<sub>x</sub> = M<sub>y</sub>, where κ<sub>x</sub> = κ<sub>y</sub> = M/[D(1 + ν)].

Numbers: a 3 mm aluminium alloy plate (E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.3) has D = 173.1 N·m. With κ<sub>x</sub> = 0.05 m⁻¹ and free edges, κ<sub>y</sub> = −0.015 m⁻¹, M<sub>x</sub> = 7.88 N·m/m and σ = 5.25 MPa; in cylindrical bending M<sub>x</sub> = 8.65 and M<sub>y</sub> = 2.60 N·m/m.

Principal moments: for M<sub>x</sub> = 10, M<sub>y</sub> = 4, M<sub>xy</sub> = 4 N·m/m, M₁,₂ = 7 ± 5 = 12 and 2 N·m/m at α = 26.6°. The principal curvatures are 0.0724 and −0.0102 m⁻¹, opposite in sign, so even with two positive moments the surface is anticlastic: M₂ < νM₁.
Rule: synclastic when M₂ > νM₁ for positive moments; anticlastic when M₂ < νM₁; cylindrical (one curvature zero) when M₂ = νM₁.
Check: Et³κ<sub>x</sub>/12 = 1890 × 0.05/12 = 7.88 N·m/m equals the free-edge M<sub>x</sub>, as the theory requires.

bank.q: Derive the governing equation of a thin plate under lateral pressure and in-plane forces, state where each term comes from, and show how compression changes the deflection of a simply supported plate.
answer: Element: a piece dx × dy of a plate with moments M<sub>x</sub>, M<sub>y</sub>, M<sub>xy</sub>, transverse shears Q<sub>x</sub>, Q<sub>y</sub>, pressure q on its face, and in-plane forces N<sub>x</sub>, N<sub>y</sub>, N<sub>xy</sub> per unit length.
Origin of the bending term: substituting M = D(κ + νκ) with κ = −∂²w gives D∇⁴w, where ∇⁴w = ∂⁴w/∂x⁴ + 2∂⁴w/∂x²∂y² + ∂⁴w/∂y⁴. It is the plate's elastic resistance.

Origin of the membrane terms: on a bent element N<sub>x</sub> acts along slopes ∂w/∂x and ∂w/∂x + (∂²w/∂x²)dx on opposite faces, leaving a normal force N<sub>x</sub>(∂²w/∂x²)dx dy. N<sub>y</sub> gives N<sub>y</sub> ∂²w/∂y², and the shear N<sub>xy</sub>, acting on all four faces, gives 2N<sub>xy</sub> ∂²w/∂x∂y.

answer.text: Governing equation (in-plane forces positive in tension):

answer: Physical reading: in a sagging plate ∂²w/∂x² < 0, so compression (N<sub>x</sub> < 0) adds to q and tension subtracts. Compression softens the plate; tension stiffens it.

answer.text: Navier solution for a simply supported a × b plate:
answer.pre:
w = ΣΣ A<sub>mn</sub> sin(mπx/a) sin(nπy/b)
A<sub>mn</sub> = 16q/[π⁶ D m n (m²/a² + n²/b²)²]  (m, n odd)
with compression N:  A<sub>mn</sub> → A<sub>mn</sub>/(1 − N/N<sub>mn</sub>)
N<sub>mn</sub> = π²D(m²/a² + n²/b²)²/(m/a)²

answer: Numbers: an 800 × 800 × 4 mm plate (E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.3) has D = 410.3 N·m. Under 1 kPa its centre deflects 4.06 mm (w = 0.00406 qa⁴/D) and M<sub>x</sub> = 30.6 N·m/m, σ = 11.5 MPa.
With 10 kN/m compression, N<sub>cr</sub> = 25.3 kN/m, N/N<sub>cr</sub> = 0.395, and the deflection grows to 6.76 mm (single-term estimate 6.71 mm). With 10 kN/m tension it falls to 2.89 mm.
Edge conditions to state: simply supported w = 0, M<sub>n</sub> = 0; clamped w = 0, ∂w/∂n = 0; free M<sub>n</sub> = 0 and V<sub>n</sub> = Q<sub>n</sub> + ∂M<sub>nt</sub>/∂t = 0.
Aircraft use: cabin pressure is q, fuselage bending gives N<sub>x</sub>, hoop tension N<sub>y</sub> and torsion N<sub>xy</sub>, so a fuselage skin panel needs every term.
Check: the magnification 1.667 is close to 1/(1 − 0.395) = 1.653, as expected near the first mode.

bank.q: Derive the critical stress of a thin rectangular plate simply supported on all edges under uniform uniaxial compression. Explain the buckling coefficient k and its dependence on aspect ratio and edge support.
answer: Set-up: a rectangular plate a × b (a along the load), simply supported on all edges, compressed by N<sub>x</sub> per unit width; isotropic, uniform thickness, elastic, initially flat.

answer.text: Governing equation with compression positive and q = 0:

answer: Edge conditions: w = 0 and ∂²w/∂n² = 0 on every edge. The shape w = A sin(mπx/a) sin(nπy/b) satisfies them.

answer.pre:
A[Dπ⁴(m²/a² + n²/b²)² − N<sub>x</sub> π² m²/a²] sin sin = 0
A ≠ 0  →  N<sub>x</sub> = π²D(m²/a² + n²/b²)²/(m/a)²

answer.text: With n = 1 (the lowest) and r = a/b:
answer.pre:
N<sub>cr</sub> = kπ²D/b²,   k = (m/r + r/m)²
σ<sub>cr</sub> = kπ²E/[12(1 − ν²)] × (t/b)²

answer: The buckling coefficient k: each m gives a curve with minimum 4 at r = m; curves cross at r = √(m(m + 1)) = 1.41, 2.45, 3.46. The plate takes the m with lowest k, so for long plates k → 4 and the buckles are nearly square.

answer.text: Values of k for long plates by edge support:

answer: Numbers: a = 1.2 m, b = 0.6 m, t = 3 mm, E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.3. D = 173.1 N·m; r = 2, so k = 6.25, 4.00, 4.69 for m = 1, 2, 3, and m = 2 controls with k = 4.
N<sub>cr</sub> = 4π² × 173.1/0.36 = 18.98 kN/m; σ<sub>cr</sub> = 6.33 MPa.

Meaning: σ<sub>cr</sub> is a bifurcation, not collapse. A plate supported on all edges carries more load after buckling by membrane tension until the stiffeners fail or the material yields. If σ<sub>cr</sub> exceeds the proportional limit, a reduced modulus is used.
Why n = 1: any n > 1 adds (n/b)² inside the bracket and only raises N<sub>x</sub>, so the plate never buckles with more than one half-wave across the load.

Second case for practice: a 450 × 300 × 2 mm skin panel (E = 72 GPa, ν = 0.33) has a/b = 1.5, between the crossing points, so k = 4.34 with m = 2 and σ<sub>cr</sub> = 12.8 MPa; a stringer flange of the same width with one free edge (k = 0.425) would buckle at only 1.26 MPa.
Check: σ<sub>cr</sub> ∝ (t/b)², so halving b would give 25.3 MPa; and the stress form 4π²E(t/b)²/[12(1 − ν²)] gives the same 6.33 MPa.

bank.q: Explain the effective sheet width of a stiffened panel after the skin buckles, derive von Kármán's formula, and explain shear lag.
answer: Panel: skin with stringers at pitch p along the load. Each bay is a plate supported along the stringer lines and buckles at σ<sub>cr</sub> = 4π²E(t/p)²/[12(1 − ν²)] = 3.62E(t/p)² for ν = 0.3.

After buckling: the middle of each bay bows out and sheds load; skin next to a stringer stays straight and keeps straining with it. The stress across a bay is high at the stringers (σ<sub>s</sub>) and low at mid-bay. Sketch: a stress curve with peaks at the stringers.

Idea of effective width: replace the real distribution by strips of total width b<sub>e</sub> per stringer at the full σ<sub>s</sub>, the rest of the bay carrying nothing, so that the load is unchanged.

answer.text: Von Kármán's derivation: the strip is just at its buckling stress when its edges reach σ<sub>s</sub>:
answer.pre:
4π²E(t/b<sub>e</sub>)²/[12(1 − ν²)] = σ<sub>s</sub>
b<sub>e</sub> = π t/√[3(1 − ν²)] × √(E/σ<sub>s</sub>) = 1.90 t √(E/σ<sub>s</sub>)   (ν = 0.3)
A<sub>e</sub> = A<sub>st</sub> + b<sub>e</sub> t,   P = σ<sub>s</sub> A<sub>e</sub>

answer: Use: b<sub>e</sub> is the total width per stringer, half on each side. If the formula gives b<sub>e</sub> > p, the stress is below σ<sub>cr</sub> and the whole bay is effective. A<sub>e</sub> is the boom area of the idealised section.

Numbers: stringers of 200 mm² at p = 150 mm on 1.5 mm skin, E = 70 GPa. σ<sub>cr</sub> = 25.3 MPa. At σ<sub>s</sub> = 100 MPa, b<sub>e</sub> = 1.90 × 1.5 × √700 = 75.4 mm, A<sub>e</sub> = 313.1 mm², P = 31.3 kN per stringer, against 42.5 kN if the skin had not buckled.
At stringer failure (250 MPa) b<sub>e</sub> falls to 47.7 mm and a panel of eight stringers carries about 543 kN.
Trend: b<sub>e</sub> ∝ 1/√σ<sub>s</sub>, so the skin load σ<sub>s</sub> b<sub>e</sub> t grows only as √σ<sub>s</sub>: the stringers take a growing share as load rises.

Shear lag: in a box beam the skin receives load from the spar webs by shear, and its shear strain makes the direct stress highest near the webs and lower mid-skin, even without buckling. It is handled by an effective width too, and matters at roots, cut-outs and load inputs.
Limits: the 1.90 assumes simply supported bay edges; riveted stringers give some restraint. The stringer must be checked separately for crippling and column buckling.
Check: at σ<sub>s</sub> = σ<sub>cr</sub> = 25.3 MPa the formula gives 1.90 × 1.5 × √(2766) = 150 mm, the full pitch, as it must.

bank.q: A simply supported aluminium alloy plate has E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.33, thickness 2 mm and loaded edge width 250 mm. Taking k = 4, find D, the critical buckling stress and load per unit width, the mode for a 750 mm long panel, and the thickness needed for a buckling stress of 20 MPa.
answer: Data: E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.33, t = 2 mm, loaded edge width b = 250 mm, simply supported, k = 4.
Plate factor: π²E/[12(1 − ν²)] = 64,609 MPa.
Critical load per unit width: N<sub>cr</sub> = σ<sub>cr</sub> t = 16.54 × 2 = 33.08 N/mm = 33.08 kN/m. Check: kπ²D/b² = 4π² × 52,370/250² = 33.08 N/mm.
Mode for a panel 750 mm long (a/b = 3): k = 4.69, 4.00, 4.34 for m = 2, 3, 4, so m = 3 and k = 4 exactly: three half-waves of 250 mm.
Effect of clamped long edges: k = 6.97 would give 28.8 MPa, an upper bound; riveted edges lie between.
Thickness for σ<sub>cr</sub> = 20 MPa: t = b √(20/(4 × 64,609)) = 2.20 mm. A 2.2 mm sheet would just do; t enters squared, so a 10% thicker sheet gives 21% more buckling stress.
Load on a 250 mm wide panel at buckling: 33.08 × 250 = 8.27 kN.

Remarks: σ<sub>cr</sub> is far below the yield stress of aluminium alloys, which is why skins are stiffened and allowed to buckle and carry load through the stringers; the elastic formula is valid because σ<sub>cr</sub> is in the elastic range.
Second mode check for a shorter panel: at a/b = 1.5 (a = 375 mm) k = 4.34 with m = 2, so σ<sub>cr</sub> = 4.34 × 64,609 × 6.400e-05 = 17.95 MPa, about 8% above the long-plate value.

Comparison with a beam strip: if the plate were treated as a pin-ended column of length 750 mm and unit width, σ = π²E(t/a)²/12 = π² × 70,000 × (2/750)²/12 = 0.41 MPa, roughly a fortieth of the plate value. The supported long edges are what make a plate so much stronger than a column of the same length.
Practical consequence: the stringer pitch, not the rib spacing, sets the skin buckling stress, which is why stringers are close and ribs far apart.
Check by units: D in N·mm divided by b² in mm² gives N/mm; 33.08 N/mm over t = 2 mm is 16.54 N/mm² = σ<sub>cr</sub>.

bank.q: An extruded angle has legs of 40 mm and 25 mm and is 1.2 mm thick, in an alloy with E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.33 and σ<sub>cy</sub> = 280 MPa. Estimate its crippling stress and load by Needham's and Gerard's methods and compare with local buckling and yield.
answer: Data: an extruded unequal angle with legs a = 40 mm and b = 25 mm, t = 1.2 mm, E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.33, σ<sub>cy</sub> = 280 MPa. Both leg edges are free.
Area: A = (40 + 25) × 1.2 = 78 mm² (corner radius neglected).
Local buckling of each leg (one free edge, k = 0.425): plate factor 64,609 MPa; long leg σ<sub>el</sub> = 0.425 × 64,609 × (1.2/40)² = 24.7 MPa; short leg 63.3 MPa. The long leg buckles first.
Gerard: g = 2 (two flanges, no cuts). g t²/A = 2 × 1.44/78 = 0.0369; √(E/σ<sub>cy</sub>) = √250 = 15.81; product 0.5838.

Comparison with yield: both crippling stresses are well below σ<sub>cy</sub> (42% and 35%), so no cut-off applies; both are four to five times the local buckling stress, showing the corner's post-buckling reserve.
Choice: the two correlations differ by about 19%, within the scatter of the test data they fit; take the lower (Gerard) for design or use test allowables for the actual section.
For a channel, Z or hat, cut through the webs into angles, give each angle its own C<sub>e</sub> (a cut edge is not free), and add the angle loads.

Local buckling of the whole angle: the long leg starts buckling at 24.7 MPa and is partly restrained by the stiffer short leg, so the section buckling stress lies between 24.7 and 63.3 MPa. Crippling at 99 to 118 MPa is far above this.

Check: the Needham value follows σ<sub>cs</sub> ∝ (b′/t)<sup>−0.75</sup>: compared with an equal 30 × 30 × 1.5 angle (b′/t = 20) in a slightly stronger alloy, the higher b′/t here gives the lower stress, as expected.

bank.q: A pin-ended channel column 1 m long has an 80 mm web and 40 mm flanges, all 2.5 mm thick (E = 70 GPa, G = 27 GPa). Find its Euler, torsional and flexural–torsional buckling loads and state which governs.
answer: Section: channel, web h = 80 mm, flanges b = 40 mm, t = 2.5 mm (mid-line); L = 1000 mm, pinned ends free to warp; E = 70 GPa, G = 27 GPa. Symmetric about x.
Area and centroid: A = 2.5 × 160 = 400 mm²; x̄ = b²t/A = 10.0 mm from the web.
Shear centre: e = 3b²/(h + 6b) = 4800/320 = 15.0 mm outside the web; x₀ = 10.0 + 15.0 = 25.0 mm, y₀ = 0.
Second moments: I<sub>x</sub> = t h³/12 + 2bt(h/2)² = 426,667 mm⁴; I<sub>y</sub> = h t x̄² + 2[t b³/12 + bt(b/2 − x̄)²] = 66,667 mm⁴.
Torsion constants: J = t³(h + 2b)/3 = 833.3 mm⁴; C<sub>w</sub> = t b³h²(3b + 2h)/[12(6b + h)] = 7.467 × 10⁷ mm⁶.
Euler loads: P<sub>x</sub> = π²EI<sub>x</sub>/L² = 294,772 N; P<sub>y</sub> = π²EI<sub>y</sub>/L² = 46,058 N.
Torsional load: P<sub>t</sub> = (GJ + π²EC<sub>w</sub>/L²)/r₀² = (22,500,000 + 51,585,132)/1858.3 = 39,866 N. Warping supplies 70% of the resistance.

answer.text: Coupled equation (bending about x with twist):
answer.pre:
(P<sub>x</sub> − P)(P<sub>t</sub> − P) − P² x₀²/r₀² = 0,   x₀²/r₀² = 0.3363
0.6637P² − 334,639P + 1.175 × 10¹⁰ = 0
P = 37,977 N (smaller root)

answer: Result: P<sub>y</sub> = 46.1 kN, P<sub>t</sub> = 39.9 kN, P<sub>FT</sub> = 38.0 kN. The flexural–torsional mode governs, 18% below the minor-axis Euler load.

Interpretation: the low J of the open section and the 25 mm offset of S from C bring the torsional mode down to the Euler range, and coupling lowers it further. Remedies: attach the stringer to skin (which restrains twist), use a closed or hat section, or brace the column more closely.

Effect of length: the warping term varies as 1/L². For a 2 m column, π²EC<sub>w</sub>/L² = 12,896,283 N·mm², P<sub>t</sub> = 19,047 N and P<sub>y</sub> = 11,515 N; for long open columns both fall, and the minor-axis Euler load soon governs again.
Order of work in an exam: section properties, shear centre, J and C<sub>w</sub>, r₀², the three uncoupled loads, then the coupled root for the axis of symmetry; state which axis couples with twist.
Check: substituting P = 37,977 N gives (294,772 − P)(39,866 − P) = 4.8507e+08 and P² × 0.3363 = 4.8507e+08, equal.

bank.q: For carbon/epoxy plies (E<sub>1</sub> = 140 GPa, E<sub>2</sub> = 10 GPa, ν<sub>12</sub> = 0.3, G<sub>12</sub> = 5 GPa, 0.125 mm thick), build the A, B and D matrices of a [+45/−45]<sub>s</sub> laminate, compare with [0/90]<sub>s</sub>, and state what each matrix does.
answer: Ply data: carbon/epoxy, E<sub>1</sub> = 140 GPa, E<sub>2</sub> = 10 GPa, ν<sub>12</sub> = 0.30, G<sub>12</sub> = 5 GPa, ply 0.125 mm. ν<sub>21</sub> = 0.0214; Q<sub>11</sub> = 140.91, Q<sub>22</sub> = 10.06, Q<sub>12</sub> = 3.02, Q<sub>66</sub> = 5.00 GPa.
Rotation: at ±45°, Q̄<sub>11</sub> = Q̄<sub>22</sub> = 44.25, Q̄<sub>12</sub> = 34.25, Q̄<sub>66</sub> = 36.23 GPa, and Q̄<sub>16</sub> = Q̄<sub>26</sub> = ±32.71 GPa, changing sign with θ.

answer.text: Laminate sums, z from the mid-plane, ply k between z<sub>k</sub>−1 and z<sub>k</sub>:
answer.pre:
A<sub>ij</sub> = Σ Q̄<sub>ij,k</sub> (z<sub>k</sub> − z<sub>k</sub>−1)
B<sub>ij</sub> = ½ Σ Q̄<sub>ij,k</sub> (z<sub>k</sub>² − z<sub>k</sub>−1²)
D<sub>ij</sub> = ⅓ Σ Q̄<sub>ij,k</sub> (z<sub>k</sub>³ − z<sub>k</sub>−1³)
[N; M] = [A B; B D][ε⁰; κ]

answer: [+45/−45]<sub>s</sub> (four plies, z = −0.25 … 0.25 mm): A<sub>11</sub> = A<sub>22</sub> = 22,126 N/mm, A<sub>12</sub> = 17,126, A<sub>66</sub> = 18,116 N/mm, and A<sub>16</sub> = A<sub>26</sub> = 0 because the ±45° plies balance.

B = 0 because the stack is symmetric. D<sub>11</sub> = 461.0, D<sub>12</sub> = 356.8, D<sub>66</sub> = 377.4 N·mm, but D<sub>16</sub> = D<sub>26</sub> = 255.5 N·mm: the +45° plies are outside, so the bend–twist coupling does not cancel.

[0/90]<sub>s</sub> for comparison: A<sub>11</sub> = 37,743, A<sub>66</sub> = 2,500 N/mm; D<sub>11</sub> = 1297.4 N·mm; no coupling terms. The cross-ply is 1.7 times stiffer in tension along x, while the angle-ply is 7.2 times stiffer in shear.

Two-ply unsymmetric [0/90]: B<sub>11</sub> = −B<sub>22</sub> ≠ 0 (about −1022 N for these plies), so an in-plane pull bends it: under N<sub>x</sub> = 10 N/mm the strip curls to a radius of about 79 mm.

What each matrix does: A relates in-plane forces to mid-plane strains (stretching and in-plane shear); D relates moments to curvatures; B couples them, so it is zero only for symmetric stacks. A<sub>16</sub>, A<sub>26</sub> couple stretching with shear (zero for balanced stacks); D<sub>16</sub>, D<sub>26</sub> couple bending with twist.
Why the order matters: A is independent of stacking order; D weights plies by z², so outer plies dominate bending, and moving 0° plies outwards raises D<sub>11</sub> greatly.
Check: for [0/90]<sub>s</sub>, D<sub>11</sub> ≈ (outer plies) 1284.3 + (inner) 13.1 = 1297.4 N·mm, matching the matrix sum.

bank.q: A 1200 mm wide compression panel has ten 150 mm² stringers at 120 mm pitch on 1.2 mm skin (E = 72 GPa, ν = 0.33). The stringers cripple at 220 MPa. Using effective width, find the panel failing load, compare with the unbuckled case, and check the rivet pitch.
answer: Data: ten stringers of 150 mm² at a pitch of 120 mm on 1.2 mm skin, panel width 1200 mm, E = 72 GPa, ν = 0.33. The stringers cripple at 220 MPa.
Sheet buckling between stringers (k = 4): σ<sub>cr</sub> = 4 × 66,455 × (1.2/120)² = 26.6 MPa. Below this the whole panel works; at the design load the skin has buckled.
Before buckling, area per stringer = 150 + 120 × 1.2 = 294 mm²; at σ<sub>cr</sub> the panel carries 78.2 kN.
At failure, σ<sub>s</sub> = 220 MPa: b<sub>e</sub> = 1.90 × 1.2 × √(72,000/220) = 2.28 × 18.09 = 41.2 mm, less than the pitch, so the sheet is buckled.
Effective area: A<sub>e</sub> = 150 + 41.2 × 1.2 = 199.5 mm²; load per stringer 220 × 199.5 = 43,889 N.
Panel failing load: 10 × 43.89 = 439 kN.
Average failing stress over the real area (10 × 150 + 1200 × 1.2 = 2,940 mm²): 149 MPa, against 220 MPa in the stringers.
Unbuckled comparison: if the skin stayed fully effective at 220 MPa the panel would carry 647 kN; buckling of the skin costs 32% of that.
Inter-rivet check at 220 MPa: s ≤ t √(cπ²E/[12(1 − ν²)σ]) = 1.2 √(66,455c/220): 41.7 mm for full fixity (c = 4), 20.9 mm for pinned ends (c = 1). A rivet pitch of about 20 mm is safe either way.
Further checks: the stringer with its effective skin as a column between ribs (Euler or Johnson), wrinkling at the attachment, and crippling of the stringer itself, which sets the 220 MPa.
Load share at failure: each stringer carries 33.0 kN itself and its effective skin 10.9 kN, so the skin provides 25% of the effective area although it is 49% of the material.
Average stress check: a panel weight-efficiency measure is P/(b t̄), with t̄ = 2.45 mm the smeared thickness; here 366 N/mm of width at t̄ = 2.45 mm.

Design changes: a thicker skin raises σ<sub>cr</sub> and b<sub>e</sub> (b<sub>e</sub> ∝ t) but adds weight in proportion; a closer pitch raises σ<sub>cr</sub> as 1/p² but needs more stringers; a stockier stringer raises σ<sub>s</sub> at failure.
Check: b<sub>e</sub> ∝ √(E/σ<sub>s</sub>): at σ<sub>cr</sub> = 26.6 MPa the formula gives 2.28 × √(2709) = 119 mm, the full pitch, as it must.

bank.q: Explain how combined compression and shear buckle a flat plate and why the interaction is a curve and not a sum of stresses. Check a 500 × 150 × 1.6 mm panel (E = 72 GPa) carrying 15 MPa compression and 25 MPa shear.
answer: Why a plate buckles in shear: pure shear equals tension and compression on the 45° diagonals; the compressed diagonal buckles, giving inclined waves.

answer.text: Single-load critical stresses (simply supported, b the short side):
answer.pre:
σ<sub>cr</sub> = k<sub>c</sub> π²E/[12(1 − ν²)] (t/b)²
τ<sub>cr</sub> = k<sub>s</sub> π²E/[12(1 − ν²)] (t/b)²,   k<sub>s</sub> ≈ 5.35 + 4(b/a)²

answer: Data: panel 500 × 150 × 1.6 mm, E = 72 GPa, ν = 0.33, σ = 15 MPa compression and τ = 25 MPa. Plate factor 66,455 MPa; (t/b)² = 1.138e-04.
Compression: a/b = 3.33; k<sub>c</sub> = (m/r + r/m)² is least for m = 3: k<sub>c</sub> = 4.045, σ<sub>cr</sub> = 30.58 MPa.
Shear: k<sub>s</sub> = 5.35 + 4(0.3)² = 5.71, τ<sub>cr</sub> = 43.17 MPa.
Interaction for a long flat panel: R<sub>c</sub> + R<sub>s</sub>² = 0.4905 + 0.3353 = 0.826 < 1, so the panel is unbuckled.
Margin for proportional loading: λ = 2/[R<sub>c</sub> + √(R<sub>c</sub>² + 4R<sub>s</sub>²)] = 1.144, MS = 0.14.

Allowable shear with 15 MPa compression: R<sub>s</sub> = √(1 − 0.4905) = 0.7138, τ = 30.8 MPa. The circle R<sub>c</sub>² + R<sub>s</sub>² = 1 would give 37.6 MPa (22% too high, unsafe); the straight line R<sub>c</sub> + R<sub>s</sub> = 1 would give 22.0 MPa (conservative).

Why a curve and not a sum: σ and τ act in different directions and buckle the panel in different wave patterns, so they cannot be added as stresses. Each is measured against its own critical value. Shear of either sign is equally damaging (the inclined wave mirrors), so R<sub>s</sub> appears with an even power; compression appears linearly because tension would help.
Other combinations, such as bending plus shear in a spar web or biaxial compression, have their own curves with different exponents from design charts.
After buckling a web carries more shear as a diagonal tension field, but a skin that supports stringers or must stay smooth is kept inside the curve at limit load.
Check: λR<sub>c</sub> + (λR<sub>s</sub>)² = 0.5611 + 0.4389 = 1.000.

bank.q: Distinguish divergence from flutter, and explain the role of natural frequency and damping in each, with numbers.
answer: Vibration basics: a mode behaves as a mass on a spring, ω<sub>n</sub> = √(k/m), with damping ratio ζ = c/(2√(km)). For the example model (500 kg, 200 kN/m, 4000 N·s/m) ω<sub>n</sub> = 20 rad/s (3.18 Hz) and ζ = 0.20.

Damping cases: ζ < 1 underdamped (decaying oscillation at ω<sub>d</sub> = ω<sub>n</sub>√(1 − ζ²)), ζ = 1 critical, ζ > 1 overdamped. Aircraft structures have ζ of a few per cent, so resonance peaks are high: 1/(2ζ) times the static response.

Natural frequency of a wing: by Rayleigh's method with φ = 1 − cos(πx/2L), a uniform 6 m cantilever with EI = 5 × 10⁶ N·m² and μ = 50 kg/m has ω ≈ 32.2 rad/s, against 30.9 rad/s exactly; the estimate is always high.

answer.text: Divergence (static). A section with aerodynamic centre a distance e ahead of the flexural axis, torsional stiffness K_θ:
answer.pre:
K_θ θ = q S e a₁ (α₀ + θ)
θ = (q/q<sub>D</sub>) α₀/(1 − q/q<sub>D</sub>)
q<sub>D</sub> = K_θ/(e S a₁),   V<sub>D</sub> = √(2q<sub>D</sub>/ρ)

answer: Numbers: K_θ = 200 kN·m/rad, e = 0.15 m, S = 4 m², a₁ = 5.7 per rad: q<sub>D</sub> = 58,480 N/m², V<sub>D</sub> = 309 m/s at sea level. Moving the flexural axis 50 mm forward raises V<sub>D</sub> to 378 m/s.

Role of frequency and damping in divergence: none directly. Divergence is a static balance of stiffness against aerodynamic moment; its speed depends on K_θ and e, not on mass or damping, and no oscillation occurs.

Flutter (dynamic): bending and torsion modes couple through unsteady air loads that lag the motion. As speed rises the two mode frequencies move together and one mode's total damping (structural plus aerodynamic) falls; at the flutter speed it crosses zero and the oscillation grows.

Role of frequency and damping in flutter: central. Well-separated bending and torsion frequencies, a high torsion frequency and mass balance ahead of the flexural axis raise the flutter speed; structural damping delays it slightly. The reduced frequency k<sub>r</sub> = ωb/V sets how much the air loads lag.
Certification: both V<sub>D</sub> and the flutter speed must lie beyond the design dive speed with a margin, shown by analysis, ground vibration tests and flight flutter tests.
Check: at q = q<sub>D</sub>/2 the twist magnification is 1/(1 − 0.5) = 2; V<sub>D</sub>² ρ/2 = 309² × 0.6125 = 58,480 N/m² = q<sub>D</sub>.

bank.q: Evaluate the design trade-offs in sizing a stiffened compression panel for a wing upper surface, covering skin buckling, effective width, crippling and material choice.
answer: Requirement: a wing upper surface carries compression from wing bending, some shear from torsion, and fuel pressure, at the lowest weight, without buckling at limit load in a way that harms the airflow or the joints, and with no failure at ultimate load.

Skin buckling: σ<sub>cr</sub> ∝ E(t/p)². Closer stringers or thicker skin raise it. Allowing the skin to buckle between limit and ultimate load saves weight, because the stringers carry the extra load and the skin works through its effective width.
Numbers (aluminium, t = 1.5 mm, 200 mm² stringers): at p = 150 mm, σ<sub>cr</sub> = 25.3 MPa; at p = 100 mm it would be 56.9 MPa, but 50% more stringers are needed.
Effective width: with p = 150 mm and stringers failing at 250 MPa, b<sub>e</sub> = 47.7 mm and the panel of eight stringers carries about 543 kN, an average of 160 MPa on its gross area.

Crippling: the stringer's own crippling stress sets σ<sub>s</sub> at failure. Thinner stringer walls cut weight but lower σ<sub>cs</sub> as (b′/t)<sup>−0.75</sup> (Needham); a 30 × 30 × 1.5 angle cripples at about 155 MPa against 300 MPa yield. Z, J and hat sections, with more corners, cripple at higher stress.
Column and flexural–torsional buckling: rib spacing sets the column length of stringer plus effective skin; open Z or channel stringers can twist, and a hat (closed with the skin) resists this.
Local checks: inter-rivet buckling sets the rivet pitch (about 25 to 50 mm for 1.2 to 1.5 mm skin at 150 to 250 MPa); wrinkling sets attachment flange sizes.

Material choice: carbon/epoxy has E<sub>1</sub> = 140 GPa at about 1600 kg/m³ against 70 GPa at 2800 kg/m³ for aluminium, so a mainly 0° laminate is several times stiffer per weight along the span. But a single 45° ply has E<sub>x</sub> of only 13.2 GPa: the laminate needs ±45° plies for shear and buckling, which lowers its axial stiffness, and B = 0 (symmetric) to avoid warping.

Composite panels are usually not allowed to buckle at limit load, because post-buckled skins can separate from stringers; they are made thicker or of sandwich construction, which raises D greatly. Damage tolerance (impact) and repair also favour thicker skins.

Conclusion: for a metal wing the lightest design lets the skin buckle above limit load, with stringer pitch and section chosen so that crippling, column and flexural–torsional failure occur at about the same load; for a composite wing the skin is kept unbuckled and laminate stacking is chosen for axial stiffness, shear and buckling together.
Check of the metal numbers: 8 × 250 × (200 + 47.7 × 1.5) = 543 kN.
